mcqs.question: Why is schema drift considered the default state of a system rather than a rare edge case?
options: Because any system with more than one team making independent changes over time will naturally add, rename, or retype fields
Because databases automatically randomize field names over time
Because schema drift only happens when a company migrates to a new database engine
Because compatibility rules force schemas to change on a fixed schedule
mcqs.explanation: Ordinary, well-intentioned software evolution — a new field for a new feature, a rename during cleanup — naturally produces schema changes over time whenever more than one team touches a system, which is nearly always. It has nothing to do with database migrations, forced schedules, or random field-name changes.

mcqs.question: A team wants to deploy a new consumer before all old-schema data has been reprocessed or expired. Which compatibility guarantee do they need?
options: Forward compatibility, so the old schema can read new data
No compatibility guarantee is needed if the consumer is deployed carefully
Backward compatibility, so the new schema can read data written under the old schema
Full compatibility is required even for this one-directional case
mcqs.explanation: Deploying a new consumer that must still read old-schema data is precisely what backward compatibility guarantees — the new schema can interpret data written under the old one. Forward compatibility protects the opposite direction, and full compatibility, while sufficient, is more than this specific scenario strictly requires.

mcqs.question: Why is JSON Schema generally considered a weaker fit than Avro or Protobuf for enforcing safe schema evolution in a data pipeline?
options: JSON Schema cannot describe nested or complex data structures
JSON Schema cannot be used with REST APIs
JSON Schema requires a paid registry service to function at all
JSON Schema is only descriptive by default — nothing stops a producer from serializing data that violates it unless external validation tooling is added
mcqs.explanation: JSON Schema documents an intended shape but doesn't enforce it during serialization the way Avro's reader/writer resolution or Protobuf's numbered fields structurally do — enforcement requires bolting on separate runtime validation, which is often skipped. It can describe complex structures fine and works well for REST APIs; the gap is specifically around automatic enforcement.

mcqs.question: A team adds a new field to an event schema and marks it required with no default value. What happens to existing consumers and historical data?
options: Nothing changes, since required fields only affect newly produced data going forward
Old data and any consumer still on the previous schema break, because there's no value to fill in for a required field with no default
The schema registry automatically backfills the missing field with a computed value
Only consumers written in a different programming language than the producer are affected
mcqs.explanation: A required field with no default has nothing to fall back to when reading data that predates the field, so both old data and any consumer still expecting the old schema fail to deserialize immediately. Registries don't invent values to backfill, and the failure isn't scoped to specific languages — it's a structural incompatibility.

mcqs.question: In the Avro v2 schema example, why does adding `discount_code` with `"default": null` keep the change backward compatible?
options: Because Avro ignores all new fields regardless of how they're declared
Because null values are not actually stored by Avro, avoiding the compatibility question entirely
Because a reader using v2 can fill in null for discount_code when reading v1 data that never had the field, instead of failing
Because backward compatibility only applies to fields of type string
mcqs.explanation: The default value gives the new reader schema a well-defined fallback for records that predate the field, so old data still deserializes cleanly — that mechanism is exactly what backward compatibility means in practice. Avro doesn't blanket-ignore new fields, defaults apply regardless of a field's type, and null is a real stored value here via the union type.
